lessons.title: 1. First Variable & String Value
lessons.description: Store text in variables using the equals sign (=).
learning_objectives: Create a variable and assign a string literal using =
lessons.starter_code:
# TODO: assign the string "Python" to the variable language
language = ""

tests.name: test_language_variable
tests.unittest_code:
def test_language_variable(self):
    self.assertEqual(language, "Python", msg="Expected variable 'language' to equal 'Python'.")

exercises.question: Which symbol is used to assign values to variables in Python?
exercises.micro_explanation: A variable stores a value that your program can use later.
exercises.worked_example_takeaway: An assignment stores the text in a variable named language.
exercises.deep_dive: In Python, assignment binds a variable name to a value in memory.
exercises.explanation: The equals sign '=' is the assignment operator in Python.

exercises.question: Assign 'Python' to variable language:
exercises.micro_explanation: Strings in Python are surrounded by quotes.
exercises.worked_example_takeaway: Quotes tell Python that the value is a text string.
exercises.explanation: Strings in Python are enclosed in quotes, e.g. "Python".

exercises.title: Assign language variable
exercises.question: Assign the string 'Python' to a variable named language.
exercises.micro_explanation: Write the variable name, followed by '=', followed by the string value.

tests.name: test_language_variable
tests.unittest_code:
def test_language_variable(self):
    self.assertEqual(language, "Python", msg="Expected variable 'language' to equal 'Python'.")

mastery_exam.question: What type of data is 'Python' in Python?
mastery_exam.explanation: Text wrapped in quotes is a string (str).

mastery_exam.question: Complete the assignment so that x holds ten:
mastery_exam.explanation: x = 10 assigns the integer 10 to x.

lessons.title: 2. Numbers & Reassignment
lessons.description: Variables can hold numbers and participate in arithmetic. There are 3 more bananas than apples, so `total_fruit` counts the apples plus 3.
learning_objectives: Assign integer values to variables and calculate totals with +
lessons.starter_code:
apples = 5
# TODO: set total_fruit to all the fruit
total_fruit = 0

tests.name: test_apples_variable
tests.unittest_code:
def test_apples_variable(self):
    self.assertEqual(apples, 5, msg="Expected apples to equal 5.")

tests.name: test_total_fruit_variable
tests.unittest_code:
def test_total_fruit_variable(self):
    self.assertEqual(total_fruit, 8, msg="Expected total_fruit to equal 8.")

exercises.question: Store the number of apples in a variable, then total the fruit:
exercises.micro_explanation: Variables store numbers without quotes, and you can add values using +.
exercises.worked_example_takeaway: Adding a variable to a number evaluates to their sum.

source.name: Python official documentation (docs.python.org) — 3.1.1 Numbers — arithmetic on numeric variables (Tutorial: An Informal Introduction)

lessons.title: 3. Recipe Preparation Calculator
lessons.description: Italian lasagna takes prep_time = 10 minutes of preparation and bake_time = 40 minutes in the oven. Keeping the given setup lines, compute total_time as the sum of prep_time and bake_time (the tests expect country == "Italy" and total_time == 50).
learning_objectives: Calculate total time by adding preparation and baking time variables
lessons.starter_code:
country = "Italy"
prep_time = 10
bake_time = 40

# TODO: set total_time to the sum of prep_time and bake_time
total_time = 0
lessons.solution_code:
country = "Italy"
prep_time = 10
bake_time = 40

total_time = prep_time + bake_time

exercises.question: Calculate total_time by adding the two existing time variables:
exercises.micro_explanation: Combine existing variables using the addition operator (+).
exercises.worked_example_takeaway: Adding the two preparation times gives the total time.
exercises.explanation: Adding prep_time and bake_time calculates the total time.

source.name: Python official documentation (docs.python.org) — 3.2 First Steps Towards Programming — variables and arithmetic

lessons.title: 4. Cinema Ticket Billing (Practice)
lessons.description: You are buying 3 movie tickets at ticket_price = 12 each plus one popcorn_price = 8 snack. Compute ticket_total = ticket_price * num_tickets, then grand_total = ticket_total + popcorn_price (the test expects grand_total == 44).
learning_objectives: Calculate ticket total using multiplication, then add popcorn cost
lessons.starter_code:
ticket_price = 12
popcorn_price = 8
num_tickets = 3

# TODO: work out the ticket subtotal, then the grand total
lessons.solution_code:
ticket_price = 12
popcorn_price = 8
num_tickets = 3

ticket_total = ticket_price * num_tickets
grand_total = ticket_total + popcorn_price

exercises.question: 3 tickets cost $12 each. Calculate ticket_total using multiplication:
exercises.micro_explanation: Multiplication (*) calculates the total cost of multiple identical items.
exercises.deep_dive: The asterisk (*) operator multiplies two numeric variables in Python.
exercises.explanation: Multiplying ticket_price by num_tickets calculates $36 total for tickets.

exercises.question: Now add the $8 popcorn price to ticket_total:
exercises.micro_explanation: Add additional costs to an existing subtotal using the + operator.
exercises.explanation: Adding popcorn_price to ticket_total gives the $44 grand total.

source.name: Python official documentation (docs.python.org) — 3.2 First Steps Towards Programming — variables and arithmetic
